blocks.text: Hypothesis testing is the formal procedure for deciding whether evidence in a sample is strong enough to overturn a default assumption about a population. Rather than asking "what number did I get," it asks "how surprising would this number be if nothing interesting were actually going on," and it gives a disciplined rule for when surprise counts as proof. It is the backbone of A/B testing, model comparison, and nearly every claim of the form "X performs better than Y" that shows up in data driven work.

blocks.alt: Overview of the hypothesis testing decision flow
blocks.caption: From research question to a reject or fail to reject decision

blocks.text: 1. The Null and Alternative Hypotheses

Every hypothesis test begins with two competing statements about the population. The null hypothesis, written H0, is the boring default: no effect, no difference, no relationship. The alternative hypothesis, written H1 or Ha, is the claim the researcher actually suspects is true: there is an effect, a difference exists, the new thing is better.

The test is built entirely around H0. Statisticians never try to directly prove H1 is true, because proving a positive claim from a finite sample is not possible with certainty. Instead the whole machine is designed to ask whether the observed data would be a reasonably likely outcome under H0. If it would not, H0 is rejected, and that rejection is treated as indirect support for H1.

blocks.title: Notation
blocks.content: H0 always contains the equality: a mean equals some value, two means are equal, a proportion equals some baseline. H1 contains the inequality: not equal, greater than, or less than. The two are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive.

blocks.text: The null hypothesis is always the conservative, no-change claim, while the alternative hypothesis is what a researcher actually suspects or hopes to demonstrate, and the entire test is structured around trying to disprove the null rather than directly prove the alternative.
2. The Logic: Assume No Effect, Look for Evidence Against It

The central logic of hypothesis testing mirrors a courtroom trial. A defendant is presumed innocent, which is the null hypothesis, and the prosecution must produce evidence strong enough to overturn that presumption beyond reasonable doubt. Nobody sets out to "prove innocence"; the trial only asks whether the evidence against innocence is strong enough to reject it.

In statistics, "innocent until proven guilty" becomes "no effect until the data says otherwise." The data is assumed, temporarily, to have come from a world where H0 is true. Then the analyst measures how unusual the observed result would be in that assumed world. An unusual result is evidence against the assumption, not proof it is false, but strong enough evidence justifies rejecting it.
2.1 Why This Indirect Approach Is Necessary

A sample can never prove a population parameter exactly equals some value, nor can it prove two groups are exactly, perfectly different. What a sample can do is show that the observed data would be extremely unlikely if the null hypothesis were true, which is a much more tractable question. This is why the conclusion of a test is phrased as "reject H0" or "fail to reject H0" rather than "H0 is false" or "H1 is proven."

items: Failing to reject H0 does not mean H0 is true, it means the data did not provide strong enough evidence against it.
Rejecting H0 does not mean H1 is proven with certainty, it means the observed data would be very unlikely if H0 were true.
The word "accept" is deliberately avoided for the null hypothesis in careful statistical writing.

blocks.text: 3. One-Tailed Versus Two-Tailed Tests

The alternative hypothesis determines whether a test looks in one direction or both. A two-tailed test asks whether a parameter is simply different from some value, in either direction, and it splits the rejection region across both tails of the sampling distribution. A one-tailed test asks whether a parameter is specifically greater than or specifically less than some value, and it places the entire rejection region in a single tail.

The choice must be made before looking at the data, based on the practical question being asked, never after seeing which direction the result happened to point. Choosing the tail after peeking at the result inflates the true false positive rate, because it silently doubles the chance of a lucky-looking result passing the threshold.

blocks.text: Choosing between a one-tailed and a two-tailed test must be decided before looking at the data, deciding afterward based on which direction the data happens to point in is a subtle but real form of bias.
4. Test Statistics: The Z-Test and the T-Test

A test statistic is a single number computed from sample data that measures how far the observed result sits from what H0 predicts, expressed in standard error units. Every hypothesis test reduces the raw data down to one such number, then compares it against a known reference distribution to see how extreme it is.

The z-test is used when the population standard deviation is known or the sample size is large enough for the sampling distribution of the mean to be treated as normal, per the central limit theorem covered in the sampling lesson. The t-test is used far more often in practice, because the population standard deviation is almost never known; it uses the sample standard deviation instead and relies on the t-distribution, which has heavier tails to account for that extra uncertainty, especially with small samples.
4.1 The One-Sample and Two-Sample T-Test

A one-sample t-test compares a single sample mean against a fixed reference value. A two-sample t-test, sometimes called an independent samples t-test, compares the means of two separate groups, such as a control group and a treatment group in an A/B test. The two-sample form is the workhorse of experimentation because most real comparisons are between two groups rather than against a fixed constant.

code.content:
import numpy as np

# One-sample t statistic: compare a sample mean to a fixed value mu0
def t_statistic_one_sample(sample, mu0):
    n = len(sample)
    sample_mean = np.mean(sample)
    sample_std = np.std(sample, ddof=1)
    standard_error = sample_std / np.sqrt(n)
    return (sample_mean - mu0) / standard_error

blocks.text: 5. The Significance Level, Alpha

Before running a test, the analyst chooses a significance level, denoted alpha, which is the threshold probability used to decide when a result counts as surprising enough to reject H0. The most common convention is alpha equals 0.05, meaning a result that would occur less than 5 percent of the time under H0 is deemed sufficiently rare to justify rejecting it.

Alpha is not a law of nature, it is a policy decision about how much false positive risk is acceptable, chosen before the data is collected. Fields where false positives are especially costly, such as clinical drug trials or safety systems, sometimes use stricter thresholds like 0.01. Exploratory or low stakes analysis sometimes tolerates a looser threshold like 0.10.

blocks.title: Alpha is a pre-registered commitment
blocks.content: Alpha must be fixed before looking at the p-value it will be compared against. Adjusting alpha after seeing the result defeats its entire purpose, since the threshold could then always be moved to whatever produces the desired conclusion.

blocks.text: 6. Type I and Type II Error

Because a hypothesis test is a decision made under uncertainty from a finite sample, it can go wrong in two distinct ways. A Type I error is a false positive: rejecting H0 when H0 was actually true, meaning the test concludes there is an effect when there really is not one. A Type II error is a false negative: failing to reject H0 when H0 was actually false, meaning the test misses a real effect that was truly there.

The probability of a Type I error is exactly alpha, by construction, since alpha is defined as the rejection threshold under H0. The probability of a Type II error is denoted beta, and unlike alpha it is not chosen directly; it depends on the true size of the effect, the sample size, the variability in the data, and the chosen alpha.

blocks.content: {"headers":["","H0 is actually true","H0 is actually false"],"rows":[["Test rejects H0","Type I error (false positive), probability alpha","Correct decision, true positive"],["Test fails to reject H0","Correct decision, true negative","Type II error (false negative), probability beta"]]}

blocks.text: The two error types trade off against each other. Lowering alpha to reduce Type I errors makes the rejection threshold stricter, which in turn makes it harder to detect a real effect, raising beta. There is no free way to shrink both simultaneously without collecting more data or using a more sensitive test design.

Lowering the significance level alpha to reduce Type I error generally increases the risk of Type II error, the two error types trade off against each other for a fixed sample size, mirroring the precision and recall tradeoff covered in the evaluation metrics module.
7. Statistical Power

Statistical power is the probability that a test correctly rejects H0 when H1 is actually true, defined as 1 minus beta. A test with low power routinely misses real effects, wasting the experiment even when the underlying phenomenon is genuine. Power depends on the true effect size, the sample size, the variability of the data, and the chosen alpha.

In practice, power is used before an experiment even runs, in a step called a power analysis, to determine how large a sample is needed to reliably detect an effect of a given minimum size. An underpowered A/B test is one of the most common causes of inconclusive experiments: the true effect may exist, but the sample was too small to detect it with confidence.

items: Larger sample size increases power, all else equal, because it shrinks the standard error.
Larger true effect size increases power, since bigger differences are easier to detect against sampling noise.
Lower variability in the underlying data increases power, for the same reason as sample size.
A convention target in experiment design is 80 percent power, meaning an 80 percent chance of detecting the assumed effect if it is real.

blocks.text: Power analysis, run before collecting data, estimates how large a sample is needed to reliably detect an effect of a given size, directly paralleling the sample size planning covered in the confidence intervals lesson.
8. Where the P-Value Fits In

Once a test statistic is computed, it gets converted into a p-value: the probability of observing a result at least as extreme as the one measured, assuming H0 is true. The decision rule is then simple: if the p-value is less than alpha, reject H0; if the p-value is greater than or equal to alpha, fail to reject H0.

The p-value lesson covers this concept in full depth, including the common misinterpretations that trip up even experienced practitioners, but the key point for hypothesis testing itself is procedural: the p-value is the single number that gets compared against the pre-chosen alpha threshold to reach a decision.
9. The Link to Confidence Intervals

Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals are two views of the same underlying calculation. A two-tailed hypothesis test at significance level alpha rejects H0 exactly when a confidence interval built at confidence level 1 minus alpha does not contain the null value. A 95 percent confidence interval and a two-tailed test at alpha equals 0.05 will always agree on the reject or fail to reject decision.

This equivalence is useful in practice because a confidence interval carries strictly more information than a bare reject or fail to reject verdict: it also shows the plausible size of the effect, not just whether zero effect can be ruled out. Many modern reporting standards prefer showing the confidence interval alongside, or even instead of, the raw hypothesis test conclusion for exactly this reason.

A confidence interval that excludes the null hypothesis value leads to the same reject decision a formal hypothesis test would reach at the matching significance level, the two tools are two views of the same underlying evidence.
10. Assumptions Behind Common Tests

Every hypothesis test carries assumptions that must hold reasonably well for its conclusions to be trustworthy. The t-test assumes the underlying data is approximately normally distributed, or that the sample is large enough for the central limit theorem to make the sampling distribution of the mean approximately normal regardless of the raw data shape. It also typically assumes observations are independent of one another.
10.1 Equal Variance and Independence

The standard two-sample t-test additionally assumes the two groups have roughly equal variance; when that assumption looks shaky, a variant called Welch's t-test is used instead, which adjusts the degrees of freedom to remain valid under unequal variances. Independence of observations is arguably the most important assumption in practice: repeated measurements on the same user, or data collected in obviously correlated batches, violate it and can badly distort the test's error rates.

blocks.title: When assumptions fail
blocks.content: If normality is badly violated and the sample is small, nonparametric alternatives such as the Mann-Whitney U test are often used instead of the t-test, since they make weaker distributional assumptions.

blocks.text: 11. Hypothesis Testing in AI and Machine Learning Practice

Hypothesis testing is the rigorous alternative to eyeballing a leaderboard. When a new model version scores 0.842 on an evaluation metric and the old one scored 0.839, that difference alone says nothing about whether the new model is genuinely better or whether the gap is just noise from the particular evaluation sample. A hypothesis test converts that question into a formal, falsifiable claim with a controlled error rate.

This shows up constantly in production machine learning. A/B testing two versions of a recommendation model, comparing a new feature against a control group for conversion rate, or deciding whether a retrained model actually reduced error rates all reduce to the same test: state H0 as "no real difference between the two versions," collect outcome data from both, compute a test statistic, and check the p-value against alpha before shipping the change.

items: Comparing click-through rate between two ranking model versions using a two-sample proportion test.
Comparing average latency or average error between an old and new model using a two-sample t-test.
Running a power analysis before an experiment to decide how many users need to see each model version.
Treating a numerically higher metric on one run as meaningless until it survives a proper significance test.

blocks.title: One run is not evidence
blocks.content: A single higher score is exactly one sample from a noisy process. Model evaluation runs, like any sample, are affected by randomness in data splits, random seeds, and evaluation subsets, so hypothesis testing exists precisely to separate a genuine improvement from a lucky draw.

blocks.text: A/B testing a new model version against the current production model is, formally, a two-sample hypothesis test comparing a metric like conversion rate or click through rate between the two groups.
12. A Full Worked Example: Does the New Webpage Design Increase Conversion Rate?

A product team redesigns a signup page and wants to know whether the new design increases the conversion rate compared to the old design. They run an A/B test: 5,000 visitors see the old design (control), and 5,000 different visitors see the new design (treatment), with each visitor recorded as converted or not.

The null hypothesis is that the new design has no effect on conversion rate, meaning the true conversion rates of the two designs are equal. The alternative hypothesis is that the new design increases the conversion rate, which makes this a one-tailed test since the team specifically cares about improvement rather than any difference in either direction. They set alpha equal to 0.05 before looking at any results.
12.1 Running the Test in Python

After the experiment runs, the control group converts at 8.1 percent and the treatment group converts at 9.4 percent. The team encodes each visitor as 1 for converted and 0 for not converted, then runs an independent two-sample t-test comparing the two groups of binary outcomes using scipy.stats.ttest_ind.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Simulated outcome arrays: 1 = converted, 0 = did not convert
np.random.seed(0)
control = np.random.binomial(1, 0.081, size=5000)
treatment = np.random.binomial(1, 0.094, size=5000)

t_statistic, p_value = stats.ttest_ind(treatment, control, equal_var=False)

print(f"control conversion rate: {control.mean():.4f}")
print(f"treatment conversion rate: {treatment.mean():.4f}")
print(f"t statistic: {t_statistic:.3f}")
print(f"p-value (two-tailed): {p_value:.4f}")

# ttest_ind reports a two-tailed p-value; halve it for the one-tailed
# test since the team only cares about treatment being greater
one_tailed_p = p_value / 2 if t_statistic > 0 else 1 - p_value / 2
print(f"p-value (one-tailed): {one_tailed_p:.4f}")

blocks.text: Suppose this run produces a one-tailed p-value of 0.018. Since 0.018 is less than alpha equals 0.05, the team rejects H0 and concludes the new design produces a statistically significant increase in conversion rate. Before shipping, they would also check the effect size and confidence interval on the conversion rate difference to make sure the improvement is not just significant but practically worth the engineering cost of the redesign.
13. Common Mistakes

items: Choosing a one-tailed test only after seeing the data point in that direction, which secretly inflates the true false positive rate beyond the stated alpha.
Treating "fail to reject H0" as proof that H0 is true, rather than as an inconclusive result that may simply reflect low statistical power.
Running a test with a tiny sample size and being surprised when a real effect is not detected, when the real issue is insufficient power.
Changing alpha after seeing the p-value so the desired conclusion is reached, which defeats the entire purpose of pre-committing to a threshold.
Ignoring the assumptions of the chosen test, such as running a standard t-test on heavily skewed data with a very small sample, and trusting the resulting p-value uncritically.

blocks.text: Peeking at results early and stopping a test as soon as it looks significant, rather than committing to a predetermined sample size in advance, inflates the true false positive rate well beyond the stated significance level.
14. Practice: Run and Interpret a Two-Sample Test

A machine learning team retrains a fraud detection model and wants to know if the new version has a genuinely lower false negative rate than the currently deployed version, not just a numerically lower one on a single evaluation run. Write the null and alternative hypotheses for this scenario, decide whether the test should be one-tailed or two-tailed, and then complete the code below to run the comparison.

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# false_negative_old and false_negative_new are boolean arrays over the
# same evaluation set, True where that example was a missed fraud case
false_negative_old = np.array([...])  # results from the deployed model
false_negative_new = np.array([...])  # results from the retrained model

# TODO: choose an appropriate test given the data is paired (same
# evaluation examples scored by both models), such as a paired t-test
# via stats.ttest_rel, and set alpha
alpha = 0.05

t_statistic, p_value = stats.ttest_rel(false_negative_old.astype(int), false_negative_new.astype(int))

# TODO: print the decision, reject H0 or fail to reject H0, by
# comparing p_value against alpha, and state it in one sentence

blocks.text: As a check on your reasoning: since both models are evaluated on the exact same set of examples, the two error arrays are paired rather than independent, which is why stats.ttest_rel is the appropriate test here rather than the independent two-sample stats.ttest_ind used in the webpage example above.

State the null and alternative hypotheses explicitly before running the test, then interpret the resulting p-value against a chosen significance level to reach a clear reject or fail to reject conclusion.
Key Takeaway

Hypothesis testing formalizes skepticism: start by assuming nothing interesting is happening, then check whether the observed data would be an unusually rare outcome under that assumption. A test statistic, a chosen significance level alpha, and the resulting p-value work together to produce a reject or fail to reject decision, always shadowed by the possibility of a Type I error, a Type II error, or simply insufficient statistical power.

In AI and machine learning work, this same machinery is what separates a genuine model improvement from a lucky evaluation run, and it is the reason A/B testing exists as a formal discipline rather than a matter of comparing two numbers and picking the larger one.
